## Description

Fixes #9058

In #9058, it was discovered that `gh repo fork` was no longer respecting the protocol of the existing remote when the user hadn't configured a git protocol. This occurred because last year a change was made so that callers fetching the git protocol from the config would always be given a default, thus it was never "unconfigured".

This bothered me a bit because the existing `Config` interface is extremely unclear about:
 * When a value is configured or not
 * Whether the value is configured by the user or is a default

I spent a lot of time going around the code trying to understand whether certain uses of this API were intentional or oversights. In many cases this lack of clarity doesn't matter but the problem is that in some cases it really does, like in `fork`. As such, instead of taking the shortest path to fixing `fork` I've tried to leave things better than when I found it by introducing some help from the type system in two ways:
 1. Being clear that a config values may not exist via an `Optional` type that **must** be handled by the caller
 2. Indicating the source of a configuration entry (`user` or `default`) that can optionally be inspected by the caller

I also took the opportunity to replace some fallible code in `config.List` with some type safe code.

## Reviewer Notes

I split the commits quite intentionally to demonstrate the introduction and use of the two major concepts. I would suggest you look at them one by one to get the idea.

### What is this? Haskell?

`Optional` types are very much at home in the ML family of languages, and are not very ergonomic in Go. I am absolutely not interested in confusing people for the sake of fancy shmancy clever code, so I'm very much open to this being rejected on those grounds.

That said from my perspective, I think using the `Optional` type in this way significantly increases maintainability and clarity. Now a caller must consider "what should I do if this config value wasn't set?"

### ConfigEntry isn't very ergonomic

Previously, the `config` methods that returned guaranteed values returned `string`s. Now they return `ConfigEntry`s which contain the `Value` and the `Source`. Most places don't care about the `Source` but `repo fork` does, only respecting the `GitProtocol` if configured by the user.

An alternative here would have been to leave those as `string` return types, and to allow `repo fork` to call `config.Get` directly. This would have required the [internal config key](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/66549fd463554ac714b77f360fda3c209c5aba98/internal/config/config.go#L18-L29) to be made public. This would have been _ok_ but the issue is that anyone else caring about the `Source` in future would have to understand this pattern. By putting the `Source` on the `ConfigEntry`, future callers at least have a hint that they might want to consider this.

### Optional Type License

I took the optional type from https://github.com/BooleanCat/go-functional which was written by a friend of mine. I copypasted it into our code base (and added the `Map` function) because I think that if we want `Optional`, we want it as a core part of our domain, closer to `stdlib` than a third party vendor. Also, it's extremely stable. This is why I added the License and Copyright notice at the top of the files.

issue_context.title: `gh repo fork` no longer respects the git protocol of the original repo when `git_protocol` is not configured
issue_context.body:
### Describe the bug

```
➜ gh version
gh version 2.49.0 (2024-04-30)
https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/tag/v2.49.0
```

In https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/1056, it was requested that `gh repo fork` respected the protocol of the existing remote i.e. if the remote was using `ssh` then the fork would as well. Later in https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/2711, it was requested that the configured `git_protocol` would take precedence over the remote, and only if no `git_protocol` was configured, we would use the protocol of the existing remote.

In #8246 the `repo fork` command [was modified to call `config.GitProtocol` rather than directly accessing the `git_protocol` config key](https://github.com/cli/cli/pull/8246/files#diff-24ae81b308c8958c24ee539bf7ff8c29be8eca722a975011c247a294a701d1ffL246). The difference here is that the `GitProtocol` method always returns the configured value or the default of `https`. However, this means that the following code branch could never be exercised:

https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/4896546432354fdf2dbf6cc06ddc26efecd471d5/pkg/cmd/repo/fork/fork.go#L257-L272

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Make a temp directory: `cd $(mktemp -d)`
2. Clone a repository via ssh: `gh repo clone git@github.com:cli/cli.git`
3. Navigate into the repository: `cd cli`
4. Fork the repository: `gh repo fork --remote=true`
5. List all remotes: `git remote -v`

#### Expected behaviour

The new fork uses the ssh protocol because the repo was originally cloned through that.

#### Actual behaviour

The fork was added using the https protocol:

```
❯ git remote -v
origin	https://github.com/williammartin/cli.git (fetch)
origin	https://github.com/williammartin/cli.git (push)
upstream	git@github.com:cli/cli.git (fetch)
upstream	git@github.com:cli/cli.git (push)
```

### Extra Details

It's worth knowing that the `git_protocol` will not be configured in the following cases:
 1. After logging in using `--with-token` and not providing `--git-protocol` e.g. `echo $TOKEN | gh auth login --with-token`
 2. After logging in using the web flow with prompting disabled e.g. `GH_PROMPT_DISABLED=true gh auth login`
 3. Running a command that uses git while using `GH_TOKEN` or another env var for authentication (and no entry in the hosts file)
comments:
### Why didn't the tests catch this?

This branch **is** covered by tests but they didn't fail when the behaviour changed because the test setup doesn't accurately reflect reality. In reality, the `git_protocol` config value can only be `https` or `ssh` but the test sets it to the empty string on line `257`:

https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/4896546432354fdf2dbf6cc06ddc26efecd471d5/pkg/cmd/repo/fork/fork_test.go#L243-L264

The consequence for this is that our config code treats this as a valid configuration with the value of empty string rather than returning `https` as it would when exercised through the CLI.

Removing this configuration stub fails as expected, with an attempt to add an `https` remote failing because the expectation is that we are adding an `ssh` remote:

```
			execStubs: func(cs *run.CommandStubber) {
				cs.Register(`git remote add fork git@github\.com:someone/REPO\.git`, 0, "")
			},
```

```
--- FAIL: TestRepoFork (0.01s)
    --- FAIL: TestRepoFork/implicit_match,_no_configured_protocol (0.00s)
        /Users/williammartin/workspace/cli/pkg/cmd/repo/fork/stub.go:27: unmatched stubs (1): git remote add fork git@github\.com:someone/REPO\.git
panic: no exec stub for `git remote add fork https://github.com/someone/REPO.git` [recovered]
	panic: no exec stub for `git remote add fork https://github.com/someone/REPO.git`
```

### What should we do about this?

Although no one has complained that we've broken them, the previous behaviour seems reasonable and we did have a regression. I'm inclined to return this behaviour to it's previous state.

I have an additional reason to believe this is the right thing to do and that is because `gh auth refresh` offers configuration of the Git Credential Manager in cases where the `git_protocol` was not set and `gh` is not the credential manager e.g.:

```
➜  cat ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml
github.com:
    users:
        williammartin:
    user: williammartin
```

```
➜  gh auth refresh
? Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? (Y/n)
```

This is a departure from `gh auth login` which only prompts for this if the user selected the `https` protocol.

review_comments: Could you explain what this line is doing?
Checks at compile time that the `Option` type satisfies the `fmt.Stringer` interface.
Wow such no longer handling unnecessary errors.

This is probably the most functional programming suspicious line. `o.Map` is a function that takes an `Optional` and provides the inner value to a function, and wraps the result of that function in an optional. This means we can take an `Option[string]` and map it to `Option[ConfigEntry]` without the manual process of unwrapping the value and creating a new `Some` ourselves.

You can think of it like `Array.map` in other languages, where the function is applies to each element of an array, and they are all wrapped up in a new array, except that it's a single element.
It sounds like a comment in this section of code might be helpful for future readers

I think what you've written is fine. Rust docs write:

> Maps an Option<T> to Option<U> by applying a function to a contained value (if Some) or returns None (if None).
That works, too.  Both read a bit like stereo instructions, requiring extra effort to look at how its used. 😅

Yeh I hear you, it's kinda unintelligible. It's probably easier to look at the [doc examples or tests.](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/7eddd537ba74e90ea141fe2f4daadbf6b9d01273/pkg/option/option_test.go#L102-L109). All that said, I don't think it's that much less clear than `Array.map`; what does mapping even mean? When you know you just kinda know.

Count yourself lucky we're not dealing in Haskell here otherwise you get magic like:

> A type f is a Functor if it provides a function fmap which, given any types a and b, lets you apply any function of type (a -> b) to turn an f a into an f b, preserving the structure of f. 🙅
